newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil current acct gap rise blamed on trade, debt.
newsitem.headline: Brazil current acct gap rise blamed on trade, debt.

text.p: Brazil's current account deficit rose sharply in the first four months of 1997 due mostly to surges in imports and remittances abroad of bond interest payments, a senior central bank official said on Thursday.
"This reflects the trade balance and growth in the deficit in the services account," said Altamir Lopes, head of the bank's economics department.

The country's January-April current account gap reached $10.722 billion, up from $5.181 billion in the same period last year, bringing the 12-month deficit to 3.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by April's end, according to central bank figures released Thursday.

The gap, continuing its rapidly widening trend since the start of the year, ballooned from $6.836 billion posted in the first quarter but was well within analysts projections of a calendar year 1997 deficit of about $30 billion.

Lopes said the deficit was pushed upward by a surge in Brazil's trade gap to $3.989 billion in the period versus $254 million a year earlier, due to soaring imports of capital goods, raw materials and automobiles.

He said the May trade deficit would be similar to April's $951 million gap but should shrink in June and July as new measures aimed at curbing imports begin to take effect and post-harvest agricultural exports increase.
"We should see it (the trade deficit) fall, maybe not in May, but in the coming months," Lopes said.
Also behind the four-month current account gap's rise was a hike in the services account deficit to $7.55 billion, from $6.071 billion in January-April 1996, the bank said.

Lopes said the services account was mainly affected by a jump in remittances overseas of profits and dividends, such as payments on Brazilian stocks and debt held by foreigners, to $2.02 billion from $619 million in the period last year.

He said Brazil's foreign reserves dropped in April to $55.288 billion from $58.120 billion in March due mostly to greater demand for foreign currency by financial institutions and debt payments to the Paris Club and private banks.

The bank paid $342 million to the Paris Club of creditor nations and $1.371 billion to private banks, including $1.259 billion in Brady debt interest, $58 million in new money bonds and $54 million in principal on EI bonds, he said.

Net foreign direct investment in Brazil reached $4.411 billion in the first four months, including $1.512 billion in April alone despite a lack of major privatizations or stock or debt offerings last month, he said.
"In April, you didn't have privatizations or anything and a billion dollars still came in," he said.
One reason was the money Brazil raised through a late April parallel bond offering on global markets, which raised $542 million, he said.

Lopes said reserves already have nearly recovered in May, due partly to a return of dollar sales by financial institutions and the privatization of Cia Vale do Rio Doce, which raised for the treasury some $1.2 billion.
Direct foreign investment so far in May has reached $1.4 billion, he said.
The bank said reserves are likely to rise this month due partly to a share offering by Unibanco in the United States and the sale a strategic stake in state power firm Cemig, he added.
